description: We are a team that aspire to sonify climate change data to help the visually impaired. Earth Science and Climate Change are two of the most important things we should be aware of in our generation. Earth Jukebox aims to achive that! It's main purpose is to educate and raise awareness. We would really appreciate any support we could receive in taking this project further, and actually causing an impact in slowing down climate change.
summary:
Earth Jukebox is a free website that turns NASA Earth data into music, so anyone can hear how any place on Earth has changed. Drop a pin on a 3D globe and pick a dataset: 12 daily NASA Earth Information Center visualizations (temperature, air quality, rain, sea temperature, fires and more) play as sound, alongside NASA POWER's climate record since 1981. Each month that runs hotter or drier than normal makes the music darker. A permutation based, shuffle-tested self-learning SI finds each place's own climate rhythms with a permutation-tested least-squares spectrum, plays them as chords, and rings a bell when a month breaks the pattern. Compare mode sets two years side by side, measures water and plants in MODIS and Landsat pictures, and writes a statistical PDF report into a public archive.

It answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge: EIC visuals become sound people can explore and check, with its GEOS values matching NASA's servers at 234 places (correlation above 0.99999). It matters because climate data lives in charts that most people never read and 2.2 billion people with vision impairment cannot fully see. With spoken guidance in 20 languages, Earth Jukebox lets students, teachers and blind users hear their own home change. Our research paper and monographs detailing the website are available in the live site: https://teamnovaquest.github.io/earth-jukebox/
Github Repository: https://github.com/teamnovaquest/earth-jukebox
details:
Earth Jukebox: hear your planet change

Climate change is the biggest story of our lifetime, yet it is told almost entirely in charts. A line rising 0.2 °C per decade is hard to feel, most people never open the data, and for the 2.2 billion people living with vision impairment, those charts can barely be used at all. We asked a simple question: what if you could listen to the Earth instead?

Earth Jukebox is our answer: a free website that turns NASA Earth data into music for any place on the planet, and then lets you check every note against the real numbers.

What it does and how it works

1. Listen to any place on Earth. Spin the 3D globe, drop a pin anywhere (your village, a glacier, a rainforest) and pick a dataset. Earth Jukebox compares every month with that place’s own normal, and the difference becomes the music’s tempo, melody and chords. Months hotter or drier than normal make the music lower and darker; healthy months sound bright. The music runs from 1981 to today, so you hear decades of change in a minute.

2. Play NASA’s Earth Information Center. Twelve daily EIC visualizations play as sound: air temperature, humidity and wind (GEOS-FP); PM2.5, ozone, carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides (GEOS-CF); rain and rain compared with the season (GPM IMERG); sea surface temperature (MUR); active fires (VIIRS); and vegetation (NDVI). Wherever possible we read NASA’s own numbers behind the pictures, not just their colours.

3. An SI that learns each place’s rhythm. Our self-learning SI trains right in the visitor’s browser on NASA POWER’s monthly record since 1981:

  • A least-squares spectrum searches 756 possible cycle lengths.
  • Each cycle must beat 99 shuffles of the data (a permutation test, p ≤ 0.05) to be kept, so nothing is found by chance.
  • The surviving cycles are fitted as a harmonic regression (sine and cosine waves plus a warming trend), then tested on five years the model never saw.
  • Each cycle becomes a musical interval, so every place has its own chord.
  • Any month more than two standard deviations from what the SI expected rings a bell. In October 2015 the Amazon was 32.1 °C against 28.5 °C expected, a +4.7σ surprise you can hear.

4. Compare any two years. Pick a place and two years. Earth Jukebox loads both years’ NASA climate data, measures water and green plants in MODIS and Landsat satellite pictures, and plays the years side by side with a “difference” track. It gives an overall verdict only when the evidence supports one. For the Aral Sea, water in the picture falls from 8.5% in 2000 to 2.0% in 2020, so 2020 is judged worse. For a lake whose water can’t be measured from comparable pictures, it says plainly that it can’t give a verdict.

5. Full research reports and a public archive. One click produces a 25-page-plus PDF research report for any place. It includes maps, Mann–Kendall trend tests with the Hamed–Rao correction, Sen’s slope, Pettitt change-point tests, natural events from NASA EONET, and NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections for 2041–2050 under two emission paths. Reports can be shared to a public archive that anyone in the world can open, read and download.

6. “Mute humans.” One button plays a place as it would sound without human-caused warming, based on published attribution science, with every simulated number clearly labelled. Hearing the gap between the two versions is often the moment climate change clicks.

7. Built for blind and low-vision users from day one. A full blind-assistance mode speaks every menu, control and result aloud. It accepts voice commands and can read audio reports, with spoken guidance in 20 languages, including Bangla, Arabic, Chinese and Spanish.

Benefits

  • Anyone can understand it. No charts or jargon are needed: if the music darkens, something changed.
  • Personal and local. It works for any point on Earth, not just big cities, so people hear their own home.
  • Accessible. Blind and low-vision people get the same climate data as everyone else, in their own language.
  • Trustworthy. Every note can be traced to a NASA number. We measured that the values we show match NASA’s own servers at 234 places, with a correlation above 0.99999 for all seven GEOS datasets. NASA’s temperature, humidity and wind also agree with ERA5 (r = 0.957–0.993). The site reproduces real events: the Aral Sea drying, Lake Mead’s decline, the 2003 Paris heatwave and the 2010 Pakistan floods. Our accuracy paper also reports where agreement is weak.
  • Free and private. No accounts, no downloads, and nothing about visitors is stored.

Intended impact

  • Students can study their own town’s climate and produce a real statistical research report.
  • Teachers can make climate change felt in a classroom in under a minute.
  • Blind and low-vision people can explore Earth science independently, many for the first time.
  • Local researchers and communities, especially in climate-vulnerable countries like our own Bangladesh, can check what is happening where they live using NASA’s data.

Hearing is the first step; acting is the next. We designed 15 buildable Physical Solutions: domestic, industrial and municipal models such as:

  • Paddy Jukebox: a solar rice-field stake that plays farmers short tunes to guide Alternate Wetting and Drying, which can cut paddy methane by up to 48%.
  • A solar warning siren mast.
  • A heat-refuge shelter and a solar cold room.

Each comes with a build guide, a financial statement, a 3D model and a presentation.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the website (about 14,000 lines); Python for the NASA data pipeline and the Physical Solutions documents.
  • Web libraries and APIs: three.js (3D globe), Leaflet (map view), Web Audio API (all music, synthesized live in the browser), Web Speech API (spoken guidance and voice commands), jsPDF (research reports).
  • Infrastructure: GitHub Pages (hosting), a Cloudflare Worker with KV storage (NASA data relay and the public archive), and Google Gemini (the SI assistant and research essays).
  • NASA data: NASA Earth Information Center (GEOS-FP, GEOS-CF, IMERG, MUR, VIIRS, NDVI), NASA POWER, GISS GISTEMP v4, MODIS and Landsat imagery via GIBS, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, and EONET. Non-NASA sources (ERA5, CAMS, NOAA, USGS, World Bank, OpenStreetMap) are used only for cross-checks and context, and are named in every report.
  • Hardware (Physical Solutions designs): ESP32-based microcontrollers, LoRa radio, solar power with battery monitoring, and audio amplifiers.
  • Video: Kdenlive for editing and an ElevenLabs AI voice for narration.

How it is creative

  • Music as the interface. Earth Jukebox is not a chart with sound added. The sound is the data, and every place on Earth gets its own chord from its own climate cycles.
  • Surprise you can hear. The bell for an unusual month turns statistics (two standard deviations) into something anyone instantly understands.
  • Listening to the world without us. “Mute humans” lets people hear an alternative Earth.
  • Solutions that sing. Even our physical devices speak the same musical language, so a farmer hears when to irrigate.

Factors our team considered

  • Honesty over drama. Simulated numbers are always labelled, and Compare refuses to give a verdict when the evidence is missing. Our papers report weak results as well as strong ones.
  • Accessibility first, not last. Blind assistance was designed alongside the main site, not added at the end.
  • Scientific rigour. We used statistical tests that hold up to autocorrelated climate data, and held-out testing so the SI is checked on years it never saw.
  • Low cost and low bandwidth. The site runs in any browser, with no installs and no accounts, which matters for students in Bangladesh and the Global South.
  • Privacy. Nothing about visitors is collected or stored.
  • Local relevance. We also focused on problems we live with in Bangladesh: heat, floods, rising seas and rice-field methane. Some of our physical build models are inspired by these problems and intended for local impact.

SI Usage Disclosure:

  1. Claude (Anthropic) helped design and write the website’s code and data handling, debug it, and draft texts. The team chose the idea, directed the features, and reviewed and tested everything.
  2. Google Gemini powers the Earth Jukebox SI assistant, Analytics, the Compare overview and the optional research essay; Gemini-written text is marked on the site.
  3. ElevenLabs provides the AI voice in our videos.
  4. Google Translate and text-to-speech voices (Microsoft Clipchamp for the spoken guides, the open-source Piper voice for audio reports) are used for translation and speech.
  5. Our own SI rhythm model runs in the visitor’s browser. It is classical statistics we wrote ourselves (a permutation-tested least-squares spectrum and harmonic regression), not a call to any outside AI service.
  6. Google Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT generated images. Our team logo was generated by Google Gemini Nano Banana 2, and both of our video thumbails by ChatGPT.

Some Important Code from Earth Jukebox:

The permutation test: how the SI proves a rhythm is real// Find the strongest cycle, then check it against 99 shuffled copies of the datavar per = 1 / G.F[bi], peak = pow[bi], ge = 0, rr = r.slice();for (var s = 0; s < SHUF; s++) { // SHUF = 99 // Shuffle: the same values in a random order have no rhythm left for (var k = rr.length - 1; k > 0; k--) { var j = Math.floor(rand() * (k + 1)), tmp = rr[k]; rr[k] = rr[j]; rr[j] = tmp; } spectrum(G, rr, shuf); // strongest "cycle" in the shuffled data var mx = 0; for (i = 0; i < G.nf; i++) if (shuf[i] > mx) mx = shuf[i]; if (mx >= peak) ge++; // count how often chance beats the real cycle}var pval = (1 + ge) / (1 + SHUF); // p-valueif (pval > ALPHA) break; // ALPHA = 0.05: not real, stop lookingP.push(per); // real: keep this cycleWhat it does: the SI looks for repeating cycles in NASA’s monthly climate record for a place. A strong-looking cycle could just be luck, so the code shuffles the same numbers into a random order 99 times; shuffling destroys any real rhythm. If the real cycle is stronger than what shuffling produces at least 95% of the time (p ≤ 0.05), it’s kept. Otherwise the SI stops. This is why Earth Jukebox never plays a rhythm that isn’t really there.The harmonic model: trend plus waves

// One row of the model for month t: a constant, a trend per decade,

// and one cosine/sine pair for every cycle the SI keptfunction design(t, P, tm) { var row = [1, (t - tm) / 120]; // 120 months = one decade P.forEach(function (p) { var w = 2 * Math.PI * t / p; row.push(Math.cos(w), Math.sin(w)); }); return row;}What it does: this is the SI’s mathematical model. Each month’s value is predicted as a starting level, plus a warming or cooling trend per decade, plus sine and cosine waves for each cycle found (the seasons, for example). The model is solved by least squares, then tested on the last five years, which it never saw during training. That’s how we know the SI predicts and doesn’t just memorize.Turning a cycle into music// Turn a climate cycle (in months) into a musical notefunction harmony(per) { var rel = 12 / per, // compare the cycle with one year oct = Math.floor(Math.log2(rel)), // which octave it falls in red = rel / Math.pow(2, oct), // fold it into one octave pq = frac(red, 8); // nearest simple fraction, e.g. 3/2 var f = 196 * Math.pow(2, oct) * pq[0] / pq[1]; // 196 Hz = G, the "yearly note" while (f < 55) f *= 2; while (f > 1760) f /= 2; // keep it audible return { ratio: pq[0] + "/" + pq[1], freq: f };}What it does: this is where science becomes music. The yearly cycle is the base note, G at 196 Hz. Every other cycle the SI finds is compared with one year and turned into the closest simple musical fraction (3/2 is a perfect fifth, 5/4 a major third). These are the same pure intervals musicians have used for centuries. Because every place has different cycles, every place on Earth gets its own chord.
